---
title: "Serfling"
---

## Overview {#sec-serfl-overview}

Every method so far has answered one question: is this week unusual for this time
of year? The Farrington chapter ended on the question that kind of method cannot
answer — has the epidemic season started? — because a normal seasonal rise is, by
construction, not unusual for its time of year. Serfling's method answers that
second question. It models what the year would look like with no epidemic in it at
all, and treats anything well above that line as epidemic activity.

A tide table works the same way. It predicts the water level from a handful of
regular cycles, each with a fixed period, and a storm surge is whatever the table
did not predict. Serfling's baseline is a tide table for a disease: a slow trend
plus a few waves of fixed length, fitted to years with the epidemics taken out, so
that an epidemic is whatever rises above it.

Robert E. Serfling published the method in 1963 at the US Communicable Disease
Center (CDC), originally to monitor weekly deaths from pneumonia and influenza (P&I)
in 108 US cities [@serfling1963]. He chose P&I deaths as the main quantitative
indicator even though excess deaths lag influenza cases by about four weeks, because
other sources such as case reports or school and work absences were not quantitative
enough or were not available on a wide scale. It is a **parametric periodic
regression** model, and sixty years on it remains one of the foundational methods for
setting epidemic thresholds [@unkel2012].

For a seasonal disease, one fixed threshold for the whole year does not work. A
threshold low enough to catch an epidemic outside the season raises alarms
continually during the peak season, while a threshold high enough for the peak
season misses epidemics outside it. Serfling solves this by letting the threshold
change over time, following the seasonal baseline.

The method rests on three main ideas:

- **Modelling the baseline:** combine a long-term trend with sine and cosine waves
  (a Fourier series) to reproduce the seasonal variation in the absence of
  epidemics.
- **Cleaning the training data:** remove or downweight past epidemic periods before
  fitting the model, so that old epidemics do not pull the baseline up.
- **Threshold and alarm rule:** set the threshold above the baseline by a margin
  measured in standard deviations of the error (usually 1.64–1.645 standard
  deviations), and confirm an epidemic only when the indicator stays above the
  threshold for at least two consecutive weeks [@serfling1963].

::: {.callout-note title="Core idea"}
Epidemic threshold = the expected level with no epidemic + a safety margin for
random variation. The variants of Serfling differ mainly in how they estimate these
two components.
:::

## Mathematical basis {#sec-serfl-math}

### The general equation {#sec-serfl-equation}

The Serfling model with $r$ harmonics has the form [@serfling1963]:

$$
E\left(Y_t\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \sum_{i=1}^{r}\left[\gamma_i\cos\left(\frac{2\pi i t}{L}\right) + \delta_i\sin\left(\frac{2\pi i t}{L}\right)\right]
$$ {#eq-serfl-general}

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $Y_t$ | Observed value of the surveillance indicator at time $t$ (cases, deaths, a percentage...) |
| $t$ | Continuous time index, $t = 1, 2, \ldots, n$ |
| $\beta_0$ | Intercept: the mean baseline level at the time origin |
| $\beta_1$ | Long-term (secular) trend coefficient, reflecting changes in population or in the reporting system |
| $L$ | Length of one annual cycle: 52 for weekly data, 13 for data aggregated into four-week periods (as in the original paper), 12 for monthly data |
| $r$ | Number of harmonics included in the model |
| $\gamma_i,\ \delta_i$ | Coefficients of the cosine and sine waves of harmonic $i$ |

: Symbols in the Serfling equation. {#tbl-serfl-symbols}

The trend need not be a straight line: a quadratic or cubic polynomial can be used
when the data change nonlinearly [@pelat2007]. In the original paper, Serfling wrote
the equation as $\hat{Y} = u + bt + \sum a_i\cos\theta + \sum b_i\sin\theta$, with
$\theta$ a linear function of $t$ [@serfling1963]; this lesson uses the symbols
$\beta$, $\gamma$ and $\delta$ to avoid clashing with notation in later sections.

### Fourier series, intuitively {#sec-serfl-fourier}

A Fourier series rests on a simple observation: any curve that repeats every year
can be assembled from sine and cosine waves of different frequencies, in the same
way that a chord is built from single notes.

- **Harmonic 1** has period $L$ (52 weeks): it rises and falls once a year.
- **Harmonic 2** has period $L/2$ (26 weeks): it rises and falls twice a year.
- **Harmonic** $i$ rises and falls $i$ times a year.

At each harmonic, the cosine–sine pair is equivalent to a single wave with a given
amplitude and phase:

$$
\gamma_i\cos\left(\frac{2\pi i t}{L}\right) + \delta_i\sin\left(\frac{2\pi i t}{L}\right) = A_i\cos\left(\frac{2\pi i t}{L} - \theta_i\right),\qquad A_i = \sqrt{\gamma_i^2 + \delta_i^2}
$$

Here $A_i$ is the amplitude (how tall the wave is) and $\theta_i$ the phase (when the
peak falls). With the cosine alone, the peak always sits at the start of the cycle;
with the sine alone, it always sits a quarter of a cycle later. Mixing the two
components in the ratio $\gamma_i : \delta_i$ lets the peak fall in any week
(@fig-serfl-fourier). The important benefit is that $\gamma_i$ and $\delta_i$ enter
the model linearly, so they can be estimated by ordinary linear regression instead
of estimating the phase by nonlinear regression.

Two points to remember:

- The analyst chooses only $L$ and $r$. The coefficients $\gamma_i$ and $\delta_i$
  (and so the amplitude and phase) are decided by the data, through the regression.
- The frequency of each harmonic is fixed. The data decide only how tall that wave
  is and where its peak falls.

::: {#fig-serfl-fourier}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-serf-fourier"></div>
```

Fourier series, illustrated. Mixing the cosine and sine of the same harmonic moves
the peak of the wave to any week; adding harmonic 2 (period 26 weeks) to harmonic 1
produces a curve with two peaks in the year, or one asymmetric peak. Change the four
coefficients; the readout converts each pair into an amplitude and a peak week.
:::

**The first-order model** ($r = 1$) gives exactly one symmetric peak a year:

$$
Y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \gamma_1\cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{52}\right) + \delta_1\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{52}\right) + \varepsilon_t
$$

**The second-order model** ($r = 2$) adds a semi-annual wave, allowing two peaks a
year or one asymmetric peak that rises fast and falls slowly (@fig-serfl-fourier):

$$
Y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \gamma_1\cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{52}\right) + \delta_1\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{52}\right) + \gamma_2\cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{26}\right) + \delta_2\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{26}\right) + \varepsilon_t
$$

Increasing $r$ lets the curve fit more complex shapes (sharp peaks, several peaks).
But if it is increased too far, the model fits random noise and leftover epidemic
peaks as well. So $r$ must be chosen by a statistical test, not by eye.

### Choosing the number of harmonics: the example in the original paper {#sec-serfl-1963}

Serfling (1963) fitted the model to P&I deaths in 108 US cities over three seasons
without a major epidemic (leaving out the 1957–58 pandemic season), with the data
aggregated into thirteen four-week periods a year [@serfling1963]. To decide whether
a second harmonic was needed, he used Bliss's analysis of variance (a partial F
test). The additional variance explained by adding harmonic 2 (mean square 8,136)
was smaller than the residual variance of the second-order model (13,157), so
$F \approx 0.62 < 1$. Harmonic 2 carried no information beyond the level of the
noise, and the first-order model was kept:

$$
\hat{Y}_t = 300.5 + 2.1\, t + 97.6\cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{13} - 2.67\right)
$$ {#eq-serfl-1963}

Here $t$ is measured in four-week periods, with origin $t = 0$ at the midpoint of the
period ending 24 September 1955. The equation is written in amplitude–phase form:
the amplitude is 97.6 deaths per week, and the peak falls at
$t = 2.67 \times 13/2\pi \approx 5.5$, around February 1956, in the middle of winter
(@fig-serfl-1963). Today the equivalent test in R is `anova(m1, m2)`; models can also
be compared by AIC [@pelat2007].

::: {#fig-serfl-1963}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-serf-1963"></div>
```

Reconstructed from Serfling (1963). (a) The baseline from @eq-serfl-1963 and an
illustrative epidemic threshold, set 1.64 times the weekly standard deviation (27.9

deviation was also corrected for the extrapolated trend, so this gap widens over
time. (b) The analysis of variance used to choose the number of harmonics. Hover
panel (a) to read any period.
:::

## Computing an epidemic threshold with Serfling {#sec-serfl-steps}

To put the equation into routine surveillance, the method goes through four steps
(@fig-serfl-steps). The goal throughout is to separate baseline variation from the
noise left by past epidemics before the threshold is computed.

::: {.algo-step}
**1. Clean the history.** Remove or downweight past epidemics before fitting, so the
baseline describes a year without them. Five ways are in use:

- **By calendar.** Drop seasons or weeks known to be epidemic. Serfling used only
  non-epidemic seasons and, when estimating the spread, replaced isolated high
  weeks with the trend value; when many years in a row had epidemics he estimated
  the trend from the low season alone, roughly mid-May to mid-September
  [@serfling1963]. EuroMOMO fits only spring and autumn weeks, when mortality is
  least affected by winter influenza and summer heat [@euromomo].
- **By percentile.** Drop a fixed share of the highest training weeks, typically
  about 15% [@pelat2007; @pelat2017]. On French influenza-like illness data the best
  configuration cut at the 86th percentile and used the full history [@souty2018].
- **Iteratively.** Fit, drop points above a boundary — the fitted line in the first
  round, the upper 95% prediction limit after that — and refit, stopping when $R^2$
  stops improving [@wang2015].
- **Robustly.** Keep every week but fit with iteratively reweighted estimation, such
  as `MASS::rlm`, so unusual weeks lose weight on their own [@pelat2017]. The CDC used
  periodic regression with a robust procedure for its P&I baseline [@cdc1998].
- **As censored.** Treat each epidemic week as left-censored — without the epidemic
  it would have been at most what was observed — and mark the week with the largest
  positive residual as epidemic, one at a time, up to a set share, about 16% for
  acute respiratory infection [@prochazka2016].
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**2. Fit and extrapolate.** Estimate the coefficients on the cleaned data, by least
squares or a weighted or likelihood variant, and project $\hat Y_t$ forward over the
weeks to be monitored. That projection is the **seasonal baseline**: what the
community should expect if nothing epidemic is going on. Five years of training is
common [@euromomo; @pelat2017], but it is a choice to be tested; on the French data
the full history did better than windows of 3, 5 or 10 years [@souty2018].
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**3. Set the threshold.** Even with no epidemic the series scatters around the
baseline, so the threshold sits a multiple of the forecast error above it:

$$ \text{Threshold}_t = \hat Y_t + z_\alpha\,\hat\sigma_t, $$

where $\hat\sigma_t$ is the standard deviation of the forecast error, estimated from
the residuals and including the extra uncertainty of extrapolating. Serfling and the
CDC use $z = 1.64$ to $1.645$ [@serfling1963; @cdc1998]; Serfling corrected the
standard deviation for the extrapolated trend but not for the Fourier terms. That $z$
is the upper end of a one-sided 95% prediction interval — equivalently a two-sided
90% one, which is `level = 0.90` in R's `predict()` [@mcconeghy_flumodelr].
Santé publique France uses the two-sided 95% limit, $z \approx 1.96$, trading
sensitivity for specificity [@pelat2017]. On a log-normal model the threshold is
computed on the log scale and transformed back, $\exp(\hat\mu_t + z_\alpha\hat\sigma)$
[@prochazka2016].
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**4. Require two weeks.** A single week above the threshold is not yet an epidemic;
one high week is as often a reporting delay or a data error as anything else. The
onset is declared only when the series stays above the threshold **two weeks in a
row** [@serfling1963; @wang2015].
:::

### What cleaning does {#sec-serfl-cleaning}

Step 1 decides the quality of the whole method. Fit raw history and every past
epidemic pulls the baseline up and swells the residual spread, so the threshold lands
too high and new epidemics are flagged late [@unkel2012]. The figure below simulates
five training seasons, each with a winter epidemic, and a sixth season to monitor;
because the data are simulated, the true baseline is known, and so is the real false
alarm rate of any threshold.

::: {#fig-serfl-steps}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-serf-cleaning"></div>
```

The four steps on simulated weekly data. Amber circles are training weeks dropped by
the trim; the grey line is the true baseline, which the method never sees. Change
the share trimmed and watch the baseline, the residual spread and the threshold move.
:::

| Trim | Residual $s$ | Baseline at the peak | Real weekly false alarm rate | Alarm before the peak |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| none | 21.9 | 30.5 above the truth | 0.05% | 1 week |
| 15% | 10.5 | 7.7 above | 2.4% | 2 weeks |
| 25% | 9.4 | 0.4 above | 5.8% | 4 weeks |
| 40% | 8.3 | 8.5 below | 18% | 5 weeks |

: What trimming does to the threshold in @fig-serfl-steps. The true noise has a
standard deviation of 10; the nominal false alarm rate is 5%. {#tbl-serfl-trim}

Untrimmed, the threshold barely fires and the epidemic is confirmed one week before it
peaks. Trim too hard and the normal seasonal peak goes too, so an ordinary week crosses
the threshold almost one time in five. The right share is roughly **the share of weeks
that are actually epidemic** — about 20% here; the common 15% was tuned on French
influenza-like illness [@souty2018]. Trimming also matters for choosing $r$: untrimmed,
the test for a second harmonic gives $F = 27.8$, because the extra wave is chasing
epidemic peaks; at 15% it falls to 1.6.

### Why two weeks in a row {#sec-serfl-twoweek}

With $z = 1.645$, an ordinary week still crosses the threshold about 5% of the time,
on average 2–3 weeks a year [@serfling1963]. Over a 26-week winter–spring with no
epidemic and independent weeks, the chance that at least one crosses is
$1 - 0.95^{26} = 0.736$. Requiring two weeks in a row leaves 25 adjacent pairs, each
crossing with probability $0.05^2$, so the chance falls to at most
$25 \times 0.0025 = 0.0625$ — exactly 0.058; Serfling quoted about one in ten.

The price is time: the chance that a genuine rise is still unflagged at the end of its
second week is 0.9 for a moderate epidemic and 0.7 for a large one, and at the end of
the third, 0.1 and under 0.01 [@serfling1963]. The arithmetic also assumes independent
weeks. Serfling noted they are slightly correlated; at a correlation of 0.4 the
two-week false alarm rate triples to about 18% (@fig-serfl-twoweek).

::: {#fig-serfl-twoweek}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-serf-twoweek"></div>
```

Serfling's argument, simulated. Each bar is one week of a 26-week season, in
standard deviations from the baseline. Amber weeks cross the line alone; red weeks
are confirmed by the week before. Simulate many seasons, then raise $\rho$.
:::

### Excess burden {#sec-serfl-excess}

Once the epidemic period has been identified, the model also estimates the excess
burden, in one of two ways:

- **Against the baseline:** $\text{Excess}_t = Y_t - \hat{Y}_t$, summed over the
  epidemic weeks [@serfling1963].
- **Against the threshold (more conservative):**
  $\text{Excess}_t = \max\left(Y_t - \text{Threshold}_t,\ 0\right)$, counting only the
  part above the threshold [@mcconeghy_flumodelr].

## Variants and practical implementation {#sec-serfl-variants}

### P&I mortality surveillance at the US CDC {#sec-serfl-cdc}

The CDC applied Serfling to the **percentage of all deaths due to pneumonia and
influenza**. Using a percentage instead of an absolute count reduces bias when the
number of reporting units changes from week to week. The baseline was projected by
periodic regression combined with a robust procedure, and the epidemic threshold was
set at 1.645 standard deviations above the baseline [@cdc1998]. From October 2016,
the data source moved from the 122 Cities Mortality Reporting System to the mortality
surveillance system of the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) [@cdc2016].

### Serfling–Poisson and EuroMOMO {#sec-serfl-euromomo}

The OLS model assumes normally distributed residuals with constant variance. That
assumption is reasonable when counts are large, but fits poorly with small or sparse
counts, or with counts stratified by age group and small area [@unkel2012]. The
solution is to move the Serfling equation into a generalised linear model (GLM) with
a Poisson distribution corrected for overdispersion (quasi-Poisson) and a log link:

$$
\log\left(\mu_t\right) = \log\left(N_t\right) + \eta_0 + \eta_1 t + \eta_2\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{52}\right) + \eta_3\cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{52}\right)
$$

Here $\mu_t$ is the expected count and $\log\left(N_t\right)$ an offset for population.
The offset is included when population data are available, so that the model
estimates a rate rather than a raw count.

This is the structure of the **EuroMOMO** algorithm (European monitoring of excess
mortality): a Poisson GLM corrected for overdispersion, with a linear trend and an
annual sine wave, fitted on the spring and autumn weeks of up to five previous years,
plus a step that corrects for delay in death registration [@euromomo]. Two extensions
are worth noting:

- **FluMOMO** puts the level of influenza activity and extreme temperatures directly
  into the model as explanatory variables [@nielsen2018].
- **The modulation model** lets the trend and the seasonal amplitude change smoothly
  over time through P-splines, instead of being fixed across years [@leger2025].

### Implementation in R {#sec-serfl-r}

| Variant | Package / function | Main syntax | Handling past epidemics and the threshold |
|---|---|---|---|
| Serfling OLS | `stats::lm`, `predict` | `lm(y ~ t + sin(2*pi*t/52) + cos(2*pi*t/52), data = df_clean)` | Trim before fitting. The threshold is the upper limit of `predict(..., interval = "prediction", level = 0.90)` [@mcconeghy_flumodelr] |
| Automatic Serfling | `flumodelr::fluserf` | `fluserf(data = df, outc = perc_fludeaths, time = yrweek_dt)` | By default fits only on June–September (treating October–May as the influenza season). Returns the baseline `y0` and the threshold `y0_ul` [@mcconeghy_flumodelr] |
| Robust Serfling | `MASS::rlm` | Same formula, fitted on a sliding 261-week window (from $w - 261$ to $w - 1$) | No trimming beforehand; the algorithm downweights unusually high weeks automatically [@pelat2017] |
| Left-censored Serfling | `survival::survreg` | `survreg(Surv(y, d, type = "left") ~ t + sin(2*pi*t/52) + cos(2*pi*t/52), dist = "lognormal")` | `d = 1`: an ordinary week; `d = 0`: an epidemic week. Iterated up to a predefined censoring share [@prochazka2016] |

: Implementing Serfling's method in R. {#tbl-serfl-r}

::: {.callout-warning title="A note on using fluserf"}
In the current source code, `y0_ul` is computed as `y0 + 1.645 × se.fit`, the standard
error of the fitted line rather than the forecast error. The resulting threshold is
therefore narrower than the threshold as the CDC defines it. Check it before using it
in operation.
:::

A minimal example of the Serfling OLS model with percentile trimming and the two-week
rule:

```r
# df: weekly data with a column y (cases); the first 260 weeks are used for training
df$t  <- seq_len(nrow(df))
train <- df[df$t <= 260, ]
clean <- train[train$y <= quantile(train$y, 0.85), ]   # drop the highest 15% of weeks

m1 <- lm(y ~ t + cos(2*pi*t/52) + sin(2*pi*t/52), data = clean)
m2 <- update(m1, . ~ . + cos(4*pi*t/52) + sin(4*pi*t/52))
anova(m1, m2)                                           # is harmonic 2 needed?

new  <- df[df$t > 260, ]
pred <- predict(m1, newdata = new, interval = "prediction", level = 0.90)
new$baseline  <- pred[, "fit"]
new$threshold <- pred[, "upr"]                          # baseline + 1.645 x forecast error
over          <- new$y > new$threshold
new$alarm     <- over & c(FALSE, head(over, -1))        # above the threshold 2 weeks running
```

## Comparison with other methods {#sec-serfl-compare}

In essence, Serfling works like a Shewhart control chart: each week is compared with
the threshold independently. This catches sudden surges well but is less sensitive to
slow, smouldering rises [@unkel2012]. This section compares Serfling with three
commonly used groups of methods.

### The Moving Epidemic Method (MEM) {#sec-serfl-mem}

MEM was developed by Vega and colleagues for influenza surveillance in Europe
[@vega2013]. Instead of one wave function for the whole year, MEM divides each past
season into three periods (pre-epidemic, epidemic and post-epidemic) based on the
maximum accumulated rate percentage (MAP) curve. The epidemic threshold for a new
season is the upper limit of a one-sided confidence interval computed from the
highest values in the pre-epidemic periods of previous seasons.

On influenza-like illness data from the French Sentinelles network, compared against
a gold standard set by expert consensus, Souty and colleagues found [@souty2018]
(@fig-serfl-compare):

- Serfling (with percentile trimming) and MEM detected the epidemic start week
  equally well.
- Serfling had higher specificity and positive predictive value, while MEM had higher
  sensitivity.
- Robust regression detected onsets less well and was the only method to split one
  epidemic season into two waves.

::: {#fig-serfl-compare}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-serf-compare"></div>
```

Performance of four methods in detecting influenza epidemics on French data (figures
from Souty et al., 2018), each at its best detector. Choose a metric.
:::

### The Farrington algorithm {#sec-serfl-farrington}

The Farrington algorithm [@farrington1996] and Noufaily's improved version
[@noufaily2013] are widely used in routine surveillance in Europe and are available in
R's `surveillance` package [@salmon2016]. Unlike Serfling, Farrington handles
seasonality **through the design of its reference window**: to compute the threshold
for week $t_0$, the algorithm takes only the data within $\pm w$ weeks of the same
point in time in the $b$ previous years (for example $w = 3$, $b = 5$), and then fits
a log-linear quasi-Poisson model:

$$
\log\left(\mu_t\right) = \theta_0 + \theta_1 t,\qquad Var\left(y_t\right) = \phi\,\mu_t
$$

Past epidemics are downweighted based on their residuals, and the threshold is
computed after a 2/3 power transformation to approximate a normal distribution, even
for small counts:

$$
U_{t_0} = \hat{\mu}_{t_0}\left\{1 + \frac{2}{3}\, z_\alpha\,\frac{\left[\hat{\phi}\,\hat{\mu}_{t_0} + var\left(\hat{\mu}_{t_0}\right)\right]^{1/2}}{\hat{\mu}_{t_0}}\right\}^{3/2}
$$

Thanks to its quasi-Poisson structure and local window, Farrington is better suited
than classical Serfling to diseases with low or sparse counts. Its limitation is that
it does not account for serial autocorrelation [@unkel2012].

### The cumulative sum control chart (CUSUM) {#sec-serfl-cusum}

CUSUM accumulates the positive standardised deviations over consecutive weeks:

$$
z_t = \frac{y_t - \mu_t}{\sigma_t},\qquad C_t = \max\left(0,\ C_{t-1} + z_t - k\right)
$$

and raises an alarm when $C_t > h$, where $k$ is the reference value and $h$ the
decision threshold [@unkel2012]. Because it accumulates information over many weeks,
CUSUM is more sensitive than Serfling to small but sustained shifts. However, standard
CUSUM does not handle seasonality on its own. If it is applied directly to seasonal
data without standardising them with a baseline model (for example, using Serfling's
residuals), it raises false alarms every time the peak season begins.

### Summary table {#sec-serfl-table}

| Method | Modelling seasonality | Handling past epidemics | Alarm threshold | Strengths | Limitations |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Serfling (OLS) | Fourier series over the whole year | Calendar exclusion, percentile trimming, robust or Tobit | $\hat{Y}_t + 1.645\,\hat{\sigma}_t$, crossed for ≥ 2 consecutive weeks | High specificity; separates trend from seasonality; easy to automate | Poor with small counts; needs regular seasonality |
| Serfling–Poisson (EuroMOMO) | Fourier series, fitted on spring and autumn weeks | Uses only weeks outside the epidemic season | Prediction interval, z-score | Suited to counts; population offset and delay correction | Assumes no excess mortality in spring and autumn |
| MEM | Splits the season into pre-, during and post-epidemic | Separates the epidemic period itself using the MAP curve | Upper limit of a one-sided confidence interval of pre-epidemic values | High sensitivity; distinguishes several intensity levels | Designed for single-peak epidemic seasons |
| Farrington | ±$w$ weeks around the same time in previous years | Downweights by residual | Threshold after a 2/3 power transformation | Suited to small counts; no assumed wave shape | Does not account for serial autocorrelation |
| CUSUM | Does not handle it alone; needs a baseline model | Resets the cumulative sum after an alarm | $C_t > h$ | Sensitive to small, sustained shifts | False alarms if the baseline model is wrong |

: Serfling compared with other methods. {#tbl-serfl-compare}

## Points to consider before applying it {#sec-serfl-apply}

Serfling's method rests on a premise about the indicator being monitored: the disease
has a clear seasonality that repeats steadily from year to year, and there is a low
baseline period long enough to anchor the estimate of the baseline [@unkel2012]. The
premise usually holds for diseases with regular seasonality, such as influenza in
temperate regions with one winter peak a year, but it is not always true. Before
applying Serfling to a specific disease, indicator or area, four points need to be
considered.

1. **There must be a low baseline period to anchor the estimate.** If a disease
   circulates all year round without any truly "non-epidemic" period, cutting out a
   fixed band of calendar weeks to obtain the baseline loses its basis, and the
   remaining data may still contain epidemic activity. For example, when estimating
   influenza-associated mortality in China, Feng and colleagues used the Serfling
   model only for northern cities with a clear winter peak; in the subtropical
   southern cities, influenza circulated all year round without a distinct season
   [@feng2012].
2. **The seasonal shape may be more complex than one peak a year.** Some diseases have
   several peaks a year, asymmetric peaks, or seasonal patterns that differ between
   regions. A first-order model (one peak a year) may then be insufficient, and the
   number of harmonics needs to be tested on each area's own data. For example, in
   northern Vietnam influenza can produce several peaks in a year, falling in
   different seasons [@horby2012], and overall the seasonality of influenza in Vietnam
   is weak [@servadio2023].
3. **The timing of the peak needs to be relatively stable between years.** The Serfling
   model uses the same seasonal wave, with a fixed phase, for every year. If the timing
   of the peak varies strongly from one year to the next, an "average" baseline built
   from previous years represents any particular year poorly, and the timing of last
   year's peak says very little about the timing of next year's. For example, in
   Vietnam the interval between influenza epidemic peaks varies much more than in
   temperate regions [@servadio2023].
4. **Performance depends on the data context.** Performance figures, such as the high
   specificity in the French study, were measured on one disease, one indicator and
   one surveillance system, so they cannot be assumed to carry over to another
   context. Before putting the method into operation, it needs to be re-evaluated on
   the historical series of the very disease and area to be monitored.

## Summary {.unnumbered}

- Serfling estimates the expected baseline with a long-term trend plus a Fourier
  series, then sets the threshold about 1.645 standard deviations of the forecast
  error above the baseline.
- Each Fourier harmonic is a cosine–sine pair, equivalent to one wave with an
  amplitude and a phase. The analyst chooses the number of harmonics $r$ by testing;
  the coefficients are decided by the data.
- Cleaning the historical data is the decisive step: if past epidemics are not
  removed, the threshold is set too high.
- The rule of crossing the threshold for two consecutive weeks reduces false alarms.
- The Poisson variant (such as EuroMOMO) is better suited to counts; Farrington and
  CUSUM complement Serfling when case numbers are small or an epidemic rises slowly.
- In tropical regions, the assumptions about seasonality need to be checked again
  before the method is applied.
